methods.title: Models and tests
methods.notes: Normal, HS and actual FHS-GJR are the main comparison. GJR is the Glosten–Jagannathan–Runkle asymmetric GARCH filter; GARCH expands to generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. UC/IND use chi-square(1); CC uses chi-square(2). A non-rejection is not proof of validity. All notation appears on the slide before use.

fhs_filter.title: FHS · Motivation and method
fhs_filter.notes:
The third model considered, for the 1-day VaR horizon, is the Filtered Historical Simulation, or FHS.

First, consider the limitations of the alternatives:

The Parametric model relies on an analytical derivation that assumes strict normality, this model is fast, but it doesn’t capture fat tails

Meanwhile, standard Historical Simulation is non-parametric, meaning it weights past data equally. This method uses real data but it’s slow to react at unexpected shock in the markets

FHS bridges these limitations with a robust, semiparametric combination.

FHS captures leverage with GJR-GARCH, filtering historical returns through conditional volatility to remove volatility clusters.

Once these historical returns are standardized and treated as independent and identically distributed, the model re-applies that volatility to future returns (of next day)

The critical advantage of this methodology is that FHS manages to retain the empirical tails of the distribution. In practice, this means we do not have to assume a clean, normal distribution; we keep the real-world extreme events found in our historical data, but we scale them dynamically to reflect current market volatility conditions.

In this way if the market suddenly enters a period of crisis, the FHS model will instantly adjust volatility upward by scaling historical shocks to reflect the new level of risk

fhs_theory.title: FHS · GJR filtering and rescaling
fhs_theory.notes:
Assume zero conditional mean: mu_t = E[r_t | F_(t-1)] = 0, where F_(t-1) is the information available before day t. Since r_t = mu_t + epsilon_t, this assumption gives r_t = epsilon_t. The forecast mean is zero; realised returns and conditional volatility can still vary.

The base model used to filter variance is the GJR-GARCH(1,1), which extends the classic GARCH model to capture the leverage effect.

sigma_t^2 = omega + beta sigma_(t-1)^2 + alpha epsilon_(t-1)^2 + gamma epsilon_(t-1)^2 I_(t-1).

sigma_t^2: conditional variance; sigma_t: conditional volatility.

ω: intercept

ϵt-12: innovation/shock

It-1: variable dummy (0 if the shock>0, 1 if the shock<0)

α: Measure the impact of new information (shocks) on volatility

β: Measures the persistence of volatility

γ: Capture market asymmetry: typically, bad news (negative returns) increases volatility more than good news does

Positivity: omega > 0, alpha and beta >= 0, alpha + gamma >= 0. Covariance stationarity with symmetric innovations: alpha + beta + gamma/2 < 1.

z_t = r_t / sigma_t = epsilon_t / sigma_t: standardized errors.

The simulated return for the following day:

tilde r_(t+1) = tilde epsilon_(t+1) = tilde sigma_(t+1) * tilde z.

fhs_limits.title: FHS · Advantages, disadvantages and asymmetry
fhs_limits.notes:
Advantages:

instant responsiveness  If there is a market crash today, the VaR calculated using FHS will be immediately higher tomorrow, providing protection for the portfolio

doesn’t assume the normal distribution

it captures leverage effect  Stock market crashes generate more uncertainty than rallies

Disadvantages:

long computation times

dependence on the historical sample  if we test a historical period without crises in the standardized residuals, the simulated paths might turn out to be too much optimistic

with extreme stress or important outliers, the parameter estimation can fail, leading to unreliable volatility

why we use the GJR-GARCH? Because the ARCH/GARCH models assume symmetry, while the GJR-GARCH consider the asymmetry

pit_definition.title: PIT and Rosenblatt Transformation
pit_definition.notes: We now move to the Probability Integral Transform, which provides a benchmark for backtesting entire forecast distributions. Applying a random variable's true continuous CDF transforms it into a Uniform(0,1) variable. In U = F_X(X), X is the random return, F_X is its true continuous CDF, and U is its percentile, uniformly distributed between 0 and 1. For historical forecast evaluation, pair each forecast made using information through day t-1 with the realised portfolio return on day t. Evaluate each realised return using its corresponding forecast CDF. The resulting percentile is u_t. The conditional PIT, or sequential Rosenblatt transformation, accounts for temporal dependence by conditioning each CDF on the past. For example, a volatile day can lead to a wider forecast for the next day. Returns may have little correlation while their volatility is persistent. Conditioning lets the forecast reflect this persistence. Conditioning alone does not guarantee independent PIT values: that is the benchmark when the conditional forecasts are correct. There is one transformation per dated forecast, not an additional transformation of the already computed PIT. Source: Diebold, Gunther and Tay (1998), https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/14779/1/SOR-98-6.pdf

pit_theory.title: PIT calibration and Normal scores
pit_theory.notes: If the continuous, one-step-ahead conditional forecast distributions are correctly specified, the PIT values should be independent and identically distributed as Uniform(0,1). We examine their uniformity as a diagnostic of marginal calibration and check temporal independence separately. Applying the inverse standard Normal CDF converts the percentiles into Normal scores. It changes their numerical values while preserving their percentile information. These scores follow N(0,1) under correct forecasts; the transformation does not force misspecified forecasts to appear Normal. Compare the ordered scores with theoretical standard Normal quantiles in a Q-Q plot. The exact theorem assumes continuous conditional CDFs. Raw empirical CDFs and estimated forecasts do not automatically satisfy it. Source: Diebold, Gunther and Tay (1998), https://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/14779/1/SOR-98-6.pdf

correct_pit.title: PIT · Changing predictive distributions
correct_pit.notes:
Each realised return moves through its own dated forecast CDF and becomes a percentile. Under correct forecasts, the accumulated percentiles should look approximately uniform. The inverse standard Normal CDF then converts these percentiles into scores that should look approximately standard Normal. The following Q-Q plot compares these scores with the standard Normal benchmark. 

Simulation with 240 changing Johnson SU true distributions and nearby, distinct predicted distributions. Both densities share one set of axes: the true unobserved density is a solid charcoal curve with light gray fill; the prediction is a slate-blue dashed curve with a thin white separation. Neither density is shifted or rescaled relative to the other. Shape, location and scale evolve at every time step. Seed 42 generates realised returns from the true distributions; every PIT is computed with its own predicted CDF, then converted to a Normal score with Phi inverse. PIT values are approximately uniform and the Normal-score histogram approximately N(0,1), rather than imposed. All 240 observations enter both histograms and the following Q-Q plot. Each particle follows its own dated CDF; faint active CDFs preserve its path while the highlighted distributions evolve. The layout follows the supplied reference: forecast CDF, PIT, inverse Normal across the top; return distribution and Normal-score histogram below. Enhanced pacing: 2 slow tracked observation(s) with actual return, PIT and Normal score before the overlapping stream; distance-weighted travel and equal arrival pauses. Labels sit outside particle paths. The bulk timeline is continuous and the empirical date readout is fixed. All observations enter the completed histograms.

correct_qq.title: Correct-specification Q–Q
correct_qq.notes:
With theoretical standard Normal quantiles on the horizontal axis and ordered transformed scores on the vertical axis, correct forecasts should produce points approximately along the 45-degree line, allowing for sampling variation. 

The 240 observations on the inverse-Normal CDF unfold directly into ordered-score Q-Q positions. X=Phi inverse((i-.5)/n); Y=the same sorted raw scores from the preceding PIT animation. The outer 5% in each tail is emphasized. The points are the same simulated-return forecast PIT scores from 240 changing Johnson SU true/forecast pairs. Forecasts are close to the true laws, so approximate Normal calibration and finite-sample departures are expected. The next demonstration changes only these Q-Q coordinates to illustrate unmodelled heavy tails.

tail_qq.title: Q–Q tail misspecification
tail_qq.notes:
Systematic departures at the extremes suggest tail misspecification. Points below the line in the left tail suggest underestimated downside tail risk. Points above the line in the right tail suggest underestimated upside tail risk. 

Only the Q-Q plot changes after the calibrated case. Scores move to centrally scaled Student-t(5) quantiles at the same plotting positions, keeping the center near slope one. Lower scores bend below the diagonal and upper scores above it. This is an explicit new pedagogical distribution, not an altered claim about the earlier sample or empirical FHS data. No second PIT animation, mean-shift sequence, or unobserved empirical tail is introduced.

empirical_pit.title: FHS-GJR · Crisis PIT · 2018–2021
empirical_pit.notes: Actual crisis-period FHS_P_J forecasts and realised returns only: 2018-01-02 through 2021-12-31, 1026 observations. GJR parameters are estimated using Gaussian likelihood; fhsVaR resamples historical standardized residuals using randi, so the final FHS forecast is empirical. One readable 2.8-second tracked example precedes an overlapping cloud of actual dated observations: 1.6-second flights, launched every .05 seconds, with about 32 simultaneous particles and quiet motion trails. Every dot follows its own actual dated forecast-CDF path. Faint active CDFs show overlapping dated laws; the solid curve and density highlight the latest launched date. No intermediate fitted forecast is invented. Every intervening observation enters both histograms and every score enters the following Q-Q plot. Diagnostics now use raw ECDF PITs. Values 0/1 correspond to returns beyond forecast support, and have infinite Normal scores. Those are shown at the animation boundary and separately marked by arrows in Q-Q plots; no arbitrary finite-rank plateau is substituted. The layout follows the supplied reference: forecast CDF, PIT, inverse Normal across the top; return distribution and Normal-score histogram below. Enhanced pacing: one tracked observation with its actual return, PIT and Normal score; distance-weighted travel and equal arrival pauses. Labels sit outside particle paths. The bulk timeline is continuous and the empirical date readout is fixed. All observations enter the completed histograms.

conclusions.title: Conclusions
conclusions.notes: Only actual GJR avoids all stress-window rejections. Normal fails stress 99% Kupiec, correcting the outline. GARCH fixes stress IND at 99%, but still rejects UC. The inference is specific to these data and windows.

limits.title: Research limitations
limits.notes: Calendar-specific results, portfolio-level filter, backward-looking inputs, selection biases and one-day horizon. No ES backtest or severity score is added. Discrete PIT corrections constrain empirical tail interpretation.
